subsystems.name: Unit cell design
subsystems.role: the repeating geometry that gives the material its unusual properties, such as stiffness-to-weight ratio or vibration damping.

subsystems.name: Base material
subsystems.role: the solid from which the lattice is made; its properties combine with the geometry.

subsystems.name: Additive manufacturing system
subsystems.role: builds the lattice layer by layer, since conventional casting or machining cannot make the internal geometry.

subsystems.name: Simulation and optimisation software
subsystems.role: predicts how the lattice will behave and iterates the design before printing.

subsystems.name: Post-processing
subsystems.role: turns the printed green part into a finished, reliable material.

subsystems.name: Integration and assembly
subsystems.role: attaches the lattice to other components or embeds it in a product.

buildSteps.title: Define target properties
buildSteps.detail: Specify what the material must do: stiffness, strength, density, energy absorption or vibration damping, plus temperature and chemical limits.

buildSteps.title: Choose a unit cell
buildSteps.detail: Select a repeating geometry — for example an octet truss, a kelvin cell or a re-entrant honeycomb (which can have a negative Poisson's ratio).

buildSteps.title: Simulate and optimise
buildSteps.detail: Use finite element analysis to predict how the lattice deforms under load. Adjust strut diameter, cell size and material distribution until targets are met.

buildSteps.title: Prepare the feedstock
buildSteps.detail: For powder-based printing, sieve and dry metal or polymer powder to a narrow particle-size range. For resin printing, mix the resin with photoinitiators and any fillers.

buildSteps.title: Print the lattice
buildSteps.detail: Build layer by layer: a laser or electron beam melts powder, or a light projector cures resin, following the sliced design. Typical layer thickness is 20–100 micrometres.

buildSteps.title: Post-process
buildSteps.detail: Remove unused powder or liquid resin, detach supports, then sinter metal parts near melting point or cure polymer parts under ultraviolet light to reach final density and strength.

buildSteps.title: Test and validate
buildSteps.detail: Measure actual stiffness, damping and strength with compression or vibration tests, and compare with the simulation. Iterate the design if needed.

buildSteps.title: Integrate into a product
buildSteps.detail: Bond, bolt or overmould the lattice into the final assembly — for example a helmet liner, a footwear midsole or a lightweight aircraft bracket.

prerequisites.why: only layer-by-layer processes can build the complex internal geometry of a lattice without moulds or cutting tools.
the behaviour of millions of struts is impossible to predict by hand; software is needed to design and optimise the unit cell.
the lattice's properties are only as good as the solid it is made from, so consistent metal powders and resins are essential.
tiny defects in a strut can change performance, so mechanical and fatigue testing is required to qualify parts.
combining stiff and soft materials in one lattice would enable multifunctional parts, but it is still mostly at research scale.

pathway.milestone: custom lattice parts in niche products such as footwear midsoles, helmet liners and aerospace brackets
pathway.unlocks: lightweighting and vibration control where conventional foams or honeycombs fall short.

pathway.milestone: faster, cheaper additive manufacturing with automated post-processing
pathway.unlocks: lattice parts in mass-market products like car interiors and consumer electronics.

pathway.milestone: multifunctional lattices that combine load bearing with cooling channels or energy storage
pathway.unlocks: compact heat exchangers and structural batteries.

pathway.milestone: programmable metamaterials whose properties can be switched on demand
pathway.unlocks: adaptive damping, morphing wings and reconfigurable medical implants.
